title: Negativity Bias
description: Negative events, emotions, and information have a stronger impact on our thoughts and behavior than equally intense positive ones.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Negative events, emotions, and information have a stronger impact on our thoughts and behavior than equally intense positive ones.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: One critical comment in a performance review overshadows ten positive ones.
You remember an insult from years ago more vividly than a dozen compliments.
News outlets lead with negative stories because they grab attention more powerfully than positive ones.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Replaying negative interactions on a loop.
Making decisions based on fear of negative outcomes rather than pursuit of positive ones.
Giving negative feedback more weight when evaluating people or options.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I know he said nine nice things, but that one thing he said stings.”
“I just can’t stop thinking about what went wrong.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Your mood is disproportionately affected by a small setback.
You dwell on what could go wrong more than what could go right.
You avoid situations because of a single past negative experience, even if overall it was positive.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Evolutionary survival required paying more attention to threats than rewards; missing a threat could be fatal, while missing a reward was merely disappointing. Baumeister et al. (2001) summarized extensive evidence: “Bad is stronger than good.”

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Deliberately count positives: after a negative event, list three good things that also happened.
When receiving feedback, ask for a balanced view; don’t let one negative bullet point dominate.
In decision making, consciously weigh upside alongside downside.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming negativity bias means you should ignore risks or negative feedback; it means you should put them in proper proportion.
Allowing it to create chronic pessimism that impairs action.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A writer publishes a blog post and receives 95 glowing comments and one harsh critique. She focuses exclusively on the critique, feeling like a failure. The next day, she reads the positive comments again, and the sting fades, but only after deliberate effort.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Your brain is Velcro for bad experiences and Teflon for good ones. To see clearly, you must press the good into memory on purpose.
